concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (infinitely many solutions)
questions.question:
If the system of equations
$x+2y+3z=3$
$4x+3y-4z=4$
$8x+4y-\lambda z=9+\mu$
has infinitely many solutions, then the ordered pair $(\lambda,\mu)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $x$ and $y$ in turn: infinitely many solutions need the coefficient of $z$ and the right-hand side both to vanish.
solution: For infinitely many solutions this equation must read $0\cdot z=0$, so $72-5\lambda=0$ and $\lambda=\frac{72}{5}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the third elimination as '(iv)$\times2-$(iii)$\times5$'; it must be (iv)$\times2-$(v)$\times5$ (the equation (v) contains $y$ and $z$ only). The values and the answer are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Infinitely many solutions means the third equation is a combination of the first two, on both sides: $R_3=pR_1+qR_2$ (augmented rows).
solution: If the system has infinitely many solutions, the augmented row $(8,4,-\lambda\,|\,9+\mu)$ is a combination $p(1,2,3\,|\,3)+q(4,3,-4\,|\,4)$.
Matching the $x$ and $y$ columns: $p+4q=8$ and $2p+3q=4$. Solving gives $q=\frac{12}{5}$, $p=-\frac{8}{5}$.

useful_results: A $3\times3$ system has infinitely many solutions iff $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}[A|B]<3$; when two rows of $A$ are independent this means the third augmented row is a combination of the other two.
Solving for the combination coefficients $p,q$ from two columns, then reading off the unknown parameters from the remaining columns, avoids every $3\times3$ determinant.
Eliminating $x$ and $y$ leaves $c\,z=d$: unique if $c\neq0$, none if $c=0,d\neq0$, infinite if $c=d=0$. Here $c=72-5\lambda$, $d=21+5\mu$.
Check of the pattern: $-\frac{8}{5}(1)+\frac{12}{5}(4)=8$ and $-\frac{8}{5}(2)+\frac{12}{5}(3)=4$, so the $x$ and $y$ coefficients of the third row $(8,4)$ are reproduced.

concepts: Unique solution and infinitely many solutions of a linear system (determinant criterion)
questions.question:
Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be respectively the sets of all $a\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ for which the system of linear equations
$ax+2ay-3az=1$
$(2a+1)x+(2a+3)y+(a+1)z=2$
$(3a+5)x+(a+5)y+(a+2)z=3$
has unique solution and infinitely many solutions. Then :
questions.key_idea: A unique solution needs $D\neq0$; a quadratic factor with negative discriminant never vanishes.
solution: Unique solution exists iff the coefficient determinant $D\neq0$.
The quadratic $15a^2+31a+37$ has discriminant $31^2-4(15)(37)=961-2220=-1259<0$ and positive leading coefficient, so it is positive for every real $a$.
So the system has a unique solution for every such $a$: $S_1=\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$.
It never has infinitely many solutions, so $S_2=\phi$. Option (B).
questions.correction_note:
The PDF only prints the value of $D$ and the line 'D $
eq a$' (a typo for $D
eq0$); it never shows why $15a^2+31a+37
eq0$. The discriminant step was added; value of $D$ and the answer are right.
useful_results: For a polynomial determinant, factor out the obvious factor (here $a$) and test the remaining quadratic with its discriminant: $b^2-4ac<0$ means no real root.
Common-factor check: when every entry of one row has the factor $a$ (row 1 here), pull it out before expanding.
Unique solution $\Leftrightarrow D\neq0$; $S_1$ is the set where $D\neq0$ and $S_2\subseteq\{D=0\}$, so $S_2=\phi$ as soon as $D$ has no non-zero real root.
Check: $a=1$ gives $D=1\cdot(15+31+37)=83$, matching direct expansion of the $3\times3$ determinant.

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (unique, no and infinitely many solutions)
questions.question:
Consider the following system of equations
$\alpha x+2y+z=1$
$2\alpha x+3y+z=1$
$3x+\alpha y+2z=\beta$
for some $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. Then which of the following is NOT correct.
options: It has no solution for $\alpha=-1$ and for all $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$
It has no solution for $\alpha=3$ and for all $\beta\neq2$
It has no solution if $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta\neq2$
It has no solution for all $\alpha\neq-1$ and $\beta=2$
questions.key_idea: Subtract the first two equations to get $y=-\alpha x$; then the third equation reduces to $(3-\alpha)(1+\alpha)x=\beta-2$.
solution: At $\alpha=-1,\beta=2$ one checks that $D_y=D_z=0$ as well, so for $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta=2$ the system has infinitely many solutions.
(A) $\alpha=-1$: $D=0$, but for $\beta=2$ the system is consistent (infinitely many solutions), so 'no solution for all $\beta$' is false. NOT correct.
(B) $\alpha=3$: $D=0$ and $D_x=2-\beta\neq0$ when $\beta\neq2$, so there is no solution. Correct.

(D) As printed ('no solution for all $\alpha
eq-1$ and $ eta=2$') is also false, since $D
eq0$ for $\alpha
eq-1,3$ gives a unique solution and $\alpha=3, eta=2$ is consistent. The Hindi text of (D) reads 'has a solution', which is true; so the intended NOT-correct option is (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF evaluates $D$ and $D_x$ only and leaves $D_y$, $D_z$ unevaluated and the four options undecided; the option-by-option verdicts were added. Also the English option (D) is a mistranslation (Hindi says 'has a solution'); as printed in English it would also be false. Key (A) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $z$ between the first two equations; then $y=-\alpha x$ and the third equation collapses to a single equation in $x$.
solution: Subtract the first equation from the second: $\alpha x+y=0$, so $y=-\alpha x$.
Put this in the first equation: $\alpha x-2\alpha x+z=1$, so $z=1+\alpha x$.
Put $y$ and $z$ in the third equation: $3x-\alpha^2x+2(1+\alpha x)=\beta$, i.e. $(3+2\alpha-\alpha^2)x=\beta-2$, i.e. $(3-\alpha)(1+\alpha)\,x=\beta-2$.
$\alpha\neq3,-1$: unique $x$. $\alpha=3$ or $-1$: the left side is $0$, so there is no solution if $\beta\neq2$ and infinitely many ($x$ free) if $\beta=2$.
So $\alpha=-1$ gives infinitely many solutions at $\beta=2$: statement (A) is the false one. Same answer.

useful_results: When $D=0$, a system is inconsistent iff some $D_x,D_y,D_z\neq0$; it has infinitely many solutions iff the rows are dependent and the augmented rows follow the same dependence.
Eliminating variables one by one reduces the system to $c\,x=d$ and makes the three cases visible at once: $c\neq0$ unique; $c=0,d\neq0$ none; $c=d=0$ infinite.
In 'which is NOT correct' options, look for the statement that claims 'no solution for ALL' values of a parameter: one exceptional value (here $\beta=2$) usually rescues consistency.
Check: $\alpha=-1,\beta=2$: $x=t$, $y=t$, $z=1-t$ satisfies all three equations (e.g. $t=0$: $(0,0,1)$ gives $1,1,2$ ✓).

concepts: Infinitely many solutions and unique solution of linear systems
questions.question:
Let the system of linear equations
$x+y+kz=2$
$2x+3y-z=1$
$3x+4y+2z=k$
have infinitely many solutions. Then the system
$(k+1)x+(2k-1)y=7$
$(2k+1)x+(k+5)y=10$
has :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions force $D=0$, which fixes $k=3$; the second system then has a non-zero determinant.
solution: For $k=3$ the second system becomes $4x+5y=7$ ... (1) and $7x+8y=10$ ... (2).
Its determinant is $4\cdot8-5\cdot7=-3\neq0$, so it has a unique solution.
(Solving fully: $x=-2$, $y=3$; $x+y=1$ and $x-y=-5$.) So the second system has a unique solution satisfying $x+y=1$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Look at the coefficient rows: row 3 $=$ row 1 $+$ row 2 in the $x,y$ columns, which fixes $k$ and consistency at once.
solution: In the first system the $x$- and $y$-coefficients satisfy $(3,4)=(1,1)+(2,3)$.
So for infinitely many solutions the third equation must be the sum of the first two: the $z$ coefficients give $2=k+(-1)$, so $k=3$.
The right-hand sides must agree too: $k=2+1=3$. Both conditions give $k=3$, consistent.
For $k=3$ the second system is $4x+5y=7$, $7x+8y=10$. Subtracting, $3x+3y=3$, so $x+y=1$; the determinant $-3\neq0$ gives a unique solution.

useful_results: If a coefficient row is the sum (or a combination) of two others, the system is consistent exactly when the right-hand sides obey the same combination.
For $2\times2$ systems $ax+by=p$, $cx+dy=q$: unique iff $ad-bc\neq0$; if $ad-bc=0$ then none or infinitely many according to whether $(p,q)$ follows the same ratio.
Subtracting two equations whose coefficients differ by $(3,3)$ gives $x+y$ directly - a quick way to test an option like '$x+y=1$' without solving.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a linear system
Quadratic equation from sum and product of roots
questions.question:
For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, suppose the system of linear equations
$x-y+z=5$
$2x+2y+\alpha z=8$
$3x-y+4z=\beta$
has infinitely many solutions. Then $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of :
questions.key_idea: $D=0$ fixes $\alpha$; then the third equation must be the combination of the first two that fixes $\beta$.
solution: With $\alpha=4$, the third equation must be a combination of the first two: $3x-y+4z=p(x-y+z)+q(2x+2y+4z)$. Matching $x$ and $y$: $p+2q=3$, $-p+2q=-1$, so $q=\frac12$, $p=2$ (the $z$-coefficient $p+4q=4$ checks).
So $\alpha+\beta=18$ and $\alpha\beta=56$; the equation is $x^2-18x+56=0$, option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops after finding $\alpha=4$ and never finds $\beta$ (needs the consistency condition, $\beta=14$); that step was written. (The second equation is printed '2a+2y+αz=8' - a typo for $2x$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Do not use determinants: eliminate $x$ and $y$ to reach $(\alpha-4)z=\text{constant}$ and force both sides to vanish.
solution: Add the first two equations: $3x+y+(\alpha+1)z=13$. Compare with the third equation: $3x-y+4z=\beta$.
From the first equation $x=5+y-z$; put in the second: $2(5+y-z)+2y+\alpha z=8$, so $4y+(\alpha-2)z=-2$ ... (B).
Infinitely many solutions need $4-\alpha=0$ and $2\beta-28=0$: $\alpha=4$, $\beta=14$. Same answer: roots of $x^2-18x+56=0$.

useful_results: For the system $a_1x+b_1y+c_1z=d_1$ etc., if the coefficient matrix has rank 2, the system is consistent iff $\operatorname{rank}[A|B]=2$; one linear condition on the right-hand sides then determines the free constant ($\beta$ here).
Two-parameter question: first the determinant fixes the coefficient parameter, then consistency fixes the constant parameter.
Roots $\alpha,\beta$ of a quadratic: use sum and product, $x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta=0$; here $4+14=18$, $4\cdot14=56$.

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (unique, no and infinitely many solutions)
questions.question:
For the system of linear equations
$x+y+z=6$
$\alpha x+\beta y+7z=3$
$x+2y+3z=14$,
which of the following is NOT true?
options: If $\alpha=\beta=7$, then the system has no solution.
If $\alpha=\beta$ and $\alpha\neq7$, then the system has a unique solution.
There is a unique point $(\alpha,\beta)$ on the line $x+2y+18=0$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions.
For every point $(\alpha,\beta)\neq(7,7)$ on the line $x-2y+7=0$, the system has infinitely many solutions.
questions.key_idea: Eliminating $x$ and $y$ leaves $(\alpha-2\beta+7)z=2\alpha-8\beta+3$: infinitely many solutions need both sides $0$ - a single point, not a whole line.
solution: From equations 1 and 3: $y+2z=8$, so $y=8-2z$, and then $x=6-y-z=-2+z$.
Unique solution if $\alpha-2\beta+7\neq0$. No solution if $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$ and $2\alpha-8\beta+3\neq0$. Infinitely many solutions if $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$ and $2\alpha-8\beta+3=0$.

(C) The two conditions $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$, $2\alpha-8\beta+3=0$ give $\beta=-\frac{11}{4}$, $\alpha=-\frac{25}{2}$: one point, and $\alpha+2\beta+18=-\frac{25}{2}-\frac{11}{2}+18=0$, so it lies on $x+2y+18=0$. True.

(D) Infinitely many solutions occur only at the single point $\left(-\frac{25}{2},-\frac{11}{4}\right)$, not at every point of $x-2y+7=0$; e.g. $(7,7)$ lies on that line but gives no solution. So (D) is NOT true.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops after listing the three cases ($\alpha-2\beta+7\neq0$ / $=0$ with $2\alpha-8\beta+3\neq0$ / $=0$) and never evaluates the four options; the option-wise verdicts (and the single point $(-\frac{25}{2},-\frac{11}{4})$) were added. Key (D) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Infinitely many solutions mean row 2 lies in the span of rows 1 and 3 (augmented); the $z$ and constant columns fix the multipliers uniquely, so only one $(\alpha,\beta)$ works.
solution: Rows 1 and 3, $(1,1,1\,|\,6)$ and $(1,2,3\,|\,14)$, are independent. Infinitely many solutions iff $(\alpha,\beta,7\,|\,3)=p(1,1,1\,|\,6)+q(1,2,3\,|\,14)$.
$z$ column: $p+3q=7$. Constant column: $6p+14q=3$. These two equations determine $p=-\frac{89}{4}$, $q=\frac{39}{4}$ - independent of $\alpha,\beta$.
Then $\alpha=p+q=-\frac{25}{2}$ and $\beta=p+2q=-\frac{11}{4}$: exactly one point gives infinitely many solutions.
This point satisfies $x+2y+18=0$ (statement C) and also $x-2y+7=0$, but a line has infinitely many points: (D) claims too much, since e.g. $(7,7)$ on that line gives no solution.

useful_results: For a $3\times3$ system whose coefficient rows other than one are fixed, the set of parameter values giving infinitely many solutions is usually a single point, not a line.
Eliminate until you get $c\,z=d$ with $c,d$ linear in the parameters: unique if $c\neq0$; none if $c=0\neq d$; infinitely many if $c=d=0$ (two linear conditions $\Rightarrow$ a point).
Quick check for 'no solution' options: set the common value and test the two conditions, as for $\alpha=\beta=7$ above.

concepts: Inconsistent system of linear equations
questions.question:
Let $S$ denote the set of all real values of $\lambda$ such that the system of equations
$\lambda x+y+z=1$
$x+\lambda y+z=1$
$x+y+\lambda z=1$
is inconsistent, then $\sum_{\lambda\in S}\left(|\lambda|^2+|\lambda|\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: A system with $D=0$ is inconsistent only if some $D_i\neq0$; check each root of $D$ separately.
solution: When $\lambda=-2$: $D=0$ but $D_1=9\neq0$, so the system is inconsistent.
When $\lambda=1$: all three equations are identical ($x+y+z=1$), so there are infinitely many solutions.
So for an inconsistent system $\lambda=-2$ only: $S=\{-2\}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF says 'When $\lambda=-2$, $D\neq0$'; this is wrong ($D(-2)=0$, as the line above it shows). It should read $D_1\neq0$ at $\lambda=-2$. Conclusion and answer 6 are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Add the three equations: $(\lambda+2)(x+y+z)=3$; subtracting pairs gives $(\lambda-1)(x-y)=0$. Both are read off without determinants.
solution: If $\lambda=-2$ this reads $0=3$, which is impossible: the system is inconsistent.
If $\lambda\neq-2$, $x+y+z=\frac{3}{\lambda+2}$ and subtracting equations gives $(\lambda-1)(x-y)=0$, $(\lambda-1)(y-z)=0$: for $\lambda\neq1$ we get $x=y=z=\frac{1}{\lambda+2}$ (a solution).
If $\lambda=1$ the three equations coincide: consistent. So $S=\{-2\}$.

useful_results: For symmetric systems $\lambda x+y+z=1$ etc., add all equations to get $(\lambda+2)(x+y+z)=\text{sum of RHS}$; this exposes the inconsistent value ($\lambda=-2$) at once.
$\begin{vmatrix} \lambda & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=(\lambda+2)(\lambda-1)^2$ (add all columns to $C_1$, then subtract).
$D=0$ does not mean inconsistent: test each root (here $\lambda=1$ gives infinitely many solutions).
Check: $\lambda=3$: $x=y=z=\frac15$ satisfies $3\cdot\frac15+\frac15+\frac15=1$ ✓.

concepts: Properties of determinants
Maximum and minimum values of trigonometric functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 1+\sin^2x & \cos^2x & \sin2x \\ \sin^2x & 1+\cos^2x & \sin2x \\ \sin^2x & \cos^2x & 1+\sin2x \end{vmatrix}$, $x\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right]$. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively are the maximum and the minimum values of $f$, then :
questions.key_idea: $R_1-R_2$ and $R_2-R_3$ create zeros and collapse the determinant to $2+\sin2x$.
solution: For $x\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right]$, $2x\in\left[\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}\right]$, where $\sin2x$ goes from $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ up to $1$ (at $2x=\frac{\pi}{2}$) and back to $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The matrix is $I+\mathbf{1}w^{T}$ (identity plus a rank-one matrix), so the matrix determinant lemma gives $f=1+w^{T}\mathbf{1}$ immediately.
solution: Each row of the matrix equals the corresponding row of $I$ plus the same row $w=(\sin^2x,\ \cos^2x,\ \sin2x)$: the matrix is $I+\mathbf{1}\,w^{T}$ with $\mathbf{1}=(1,1,1)^{T}$.

useful_results: Matrix determinant lemma: $\det(A+uv^{T})=\det A\,(1+v^{T}A^{-1}u)$; with $A=I$: $\det(I+uv^{T})=1+v^{T}u$. Whenever every row equals a fixed row plus a standard basis row, use it.
Row operations $R_i\to R_i-R_{i+1}$ often create two zeros in each row when neighbouring rows differ in few entries.
For $\sin2x$ on $x\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right]$ the maximum is at the interior point $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and the minimum is at an endpoint (both ends give $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$).

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (unique, no and infinitely many solutions)
questions.question: For the system of linear equations $\alpha x+y+z=1$, $x+\alpha y+z=1$, $x+y+\alpha z=\beta$, which one of the following statements is NOT true?
options: It has infinitely many solutions if $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=1$
It has no solution if $\alpha=-2$ and $\beta=1$
It has infinitely many solutions if $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=-1$
questions.key_idea: $D=(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha+2)$ is non-zero at $\alpha=2$, so the system is uniquely solvable whatever $\beta$ is.
solution: (A) $\alpha=1$: all three equations become $x+y+z=1$ (if $\beta=1$), so there are infinitely many solutions. True.
(B) $\alpha=2$, $\beta=1$: $D=4\neq0$, so a unique solution; adding the three equations, $(\alpha+2)(x+y+z)=2+\beta$ gives $4(x+y+z)=3$, so $x+y+z=\frac34$. True.
(C) $\alpha=-2$, $\beta=1$: $D=0$; adding the three equations gives $0=3$, so there is no solution. True.
(D) $\alpha=2$, $\beta=-1$: $D=4\neq0$, so the system has a unique solution (namely $x=y=\frac34$, $z=-\frac54$), not infinitely many. So (D) is NOT true.
questions.correction_note: The PDF says that for $\alpha=2,\beta=-1$ the system '$2x+y+z=1,\ x+2y+z=1,\ x+y+2z=-1$' has 'No solution'. This is wrong: $D=4\neq0$, so it has the unique solution $\left(\frac34,\frac34,-\frac54\right)$. Option (D) is still the false statement, so the key is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Add the equations and subtract them in pairs: $(\alpha+2)(x+y+z)=2+\beta$ and $(\alpha-1)(x-y)=0$, $(\alpha-1)(y-z)=1-\beta$.
solution: Subtracting the first two: $(\alpha-1)(x-y)=0$. Subtracting the last two: $(\alpha-1)(y-z)=1-\beta$.
$\alpha=-2,\beta=1$: the sum equation reads $0=3$: no solution (C). $\alpha=1,\beta=1$: the difference equations are $0=0$ and $0=0$ and the sum equation is $3(x+y+z)=3$: infinitely many (A).
$\alpha=2,\beta=-1$: $x=y$, $y-z=2$ and $4(x+y+z)=1$, i.e. one solution $x=y=\frac34$, $z=-\frac54$: unique, so (D) is false. Same answer.

useful_results: For a system with the cyclic pattern $\alpha x+y+z$, $x+\alpha y+z$, $x+y+\alpha z$: $D=(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha+2)$; the exceptional values are $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=-2$ only.
At $\alpha=-2$ the equations add to $0=2+\beta$: consistent only for $\beta=-2$ (then infinitely many solutions); at $\alpha=1$ they say $x+y+z=1,1,\beta$: consistent only for $\beta=1$.
A non-zero $D$ always means a unique solution, no matter what the right-hand side is - this rules out 'no solution' / 'infinitely many' options immediately.
Check: $(\alpha,\beta)=(2,-1)$, $(x,y,z)=(\frac34,\frac34,-\frac54)$: $\frac32+\frac34-\frac54=1$ ✓, $\frac34+\frac32-\frac54=1$ ✓, $\frac34+\frac34-\frac52=-1$ ✓.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a linear system
questions.question:
If the system of equations
$x+y+az=b$
$2x+5y+2z=6$
$x+2y+3z=3$
has infinitely many solutions, then $2a+3b$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions need $\Delta=\Delta_x=\Delta_y=\Delta_z=0$; $\Delta=0$ fixes $a$ and $\Delta_z=0$ fixes $b$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate by row operations: the first row must reduce to $0=0$ after removing the other two rows' multiples.
solution: Row 2 $-2\times$ row 3 gives $y-4z=0$, so $y=4z$. This does not involve $a$ or $b$.
Infinitely many solutions need $(a-7)=0$ and $b-3=0$: $a=7$, $b=3$, so $2a+3b=23$. Same answer.

useful_results: Eliminating variables in the two 'known' equations first and then substituting into the 'unknown' equation reduces the question to $(\text{coefficient})\,z=(\text{constant})$, requiring both to be $0$.

When $\Delta=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}A=2$, the numbers $\Delta_x,\Delta_y,\Delta_z$ are all multiples of one quantity, so it is enough to test one whose multiplier is non-zero (here $\Delta_z$, which contains $-b+3$).

A non-zero $2\times2$ minor, here $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}=-1$, shows $\operatorname{rank}A\ge2$ for every $a$; so 'infinitely many solutions' means rank $2$ with a one-parameter family.

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (unique, no and infinitely many solutions)
questions.question:
For the system of equations
$x+y+z=6$
$x+2y+\alpha z=10$
$x+3y+5z=\beta$,
which one of the following is NOT true?
options: System has a unique solution for $\alpha=-3$, $\beta=14$
System has a unique solution for $\alpha=-3$, $\beta\neq14$
System has infinitely many solutions for $\alpha=3$, $\beta=14$
questions.answer: Key: (D) - but all four statements are true as printed (see solution)
questions.key_idea: Subtracting equations pairwise gives $(6-2\alpha)z=\beta-14$, which settles every statement at once.
solution: $D\neq0\Leftrightarrow\alpha\neq3$: then the solution is unique, whatever $\beta$ is.
(A) $\alpha=-3$: $D=12\neq0$, so a unique solution for every $\beta$, including $\beta=14$. True.
For $\alpha=3$ ($D=0$): equation 2 $-$ equation 1 gives $y+2z=4$ and equation 3 $-$ equation 2 gives $y+2z=\beta-10$.
(C) $\alpha=3$, $\beta=24$: the two results read $y+2z=4$ and $y+2z=14$, which contradict; no solution. True.
(D) $\alpha=3$, $\beta=14$: both read $y+2z=4$; so $y=4-2z$, $x=6-y-z=2+z$ with $z$ free: infinitely many solutions. True.
So as printed every statement is true; the PDF's key (D) is not supported. (The Hindi wording of (A) appears to say 'does not have a unique solution', which would make (A) the NOT-true statement.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF only computes $D=6-2\alpha$ and the line 'unique solution $\Rightarrow\alpha\neq3$', then stops; no option is decided. Evaluating all four options shows that every one is true as printed (key (D) is true: $\alpha=3,\beta=14$ gives infinitely many solutions). The answer key looks wrong or the question is misprinted; Hindi (A) reads 'no unique solution', which would make (A) the answer.

It has infinitely many solutions if $a=3$, $b=6$

questions.question:
If the system of equations
$x+\left(\sqrt2\sin\alpha\right)y+\left(\sqrt2\cos\alpha\right)z=0$
$x+(\cos\alpha)y+(\sin\alpha)z=0$
$x+(\sin\alpha)y-(\cos\alpha)z=0$
has a non-trivial solution, then $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $D=0$ reduces to $\cos2\alpha-\sin2\alpha=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, i.e. $\cos\left(2\alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=-\frac12$.
solution: For $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$: $n=0$ with $+$ gives $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{8}=\frac{5\pi}{24}$; $n=0$ with $-$ is negative and $n=1$ with $-$ gives $\frac{13\pi}{24}>\frac{\pi}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ first: subtracting equations leaves two equations in $y,z$ only, whose $2\times2$ determinant must vanish (else $y=z=0$ and then $x=0$).
solution: A non-trivial $(x,y,z)$ needs $(y,z)\neq(0,0)$ (if $y=z=0$ then $x=0$), so the $2\times2$ determinant of these two equations is $0$.

useful_results: $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta=R\cos(\theta-\phi)$ with $R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: here $\cos2\alpha-\sin2\alpha=\sqrt2\cos\left(2\alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$.
$\cos\theta=\cos\phi\Leftrightarrow\theta=2n\pi\pm\phi$; always filter the solutions with the given interval ($\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ keeps only one).
Eliminating the variable with equal coefficients ($x$ has coefficient $1$ everywhere) reduces a $3\times3$ homogeneous determinant to a $2\times2$.
Check: $\alpha=\frac{5\pi}{24}$: $2\alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12$ ✓.

questions.question:
The values of $m,n$, for which the system of equations
$x+y+z=4$,
$2x+5y+5z=17$,
$x+2y+mz=n$
has infinitely many solutions, satisfy the equation :
questions.key_idea: Row-reduce the augmented matrix: after $R_3-\frac13R_2$ the last row must be $(0,0,0\,|\,0)$.
solution: Write the augmented matrix $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 & 5 & 17 \\ 1 & 2 & m & n \end{array}\right]$.
Apply $R_2\to R_2-2R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & m-1 & n-4 \end{array}\right]$.
Divide $R_2$ by $3$: the second row becomes $(0,1,1\,|\,3)$.
For infinitely many solutions the third row must equal the second: $m-1=1$ and $n-4=3$, so $m=2$ and $n=7$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Third row $=\frac13R_1+\frac13R_2$ in the $x,y$ columns: the $z$ column and the constants then give $m,n$ directly.

useful_results: For a system $Ax=b$ with an unknown last row $(1,2,m\,|\,n)$: infinitely many solutions iff that row lies in the span of the other augmented rows.
Row-echelon form is the quickest test: a row $(0,0,c\,|\,d)$ gives $c\,z=d$; $c=d=0$ means a free variable.
With integer $m,n$ found, test each option by direct substitution: (A) $4+49-2-7=44\neq46$, (C) $4+49+2+7=62\neq64$, (B) $=39$ ✓.

questions.question: For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and a natural number $n$, let $A_r=\begin{vmatrix} r & 1 & \frac{n^2}{2}+\alpha \\ 2r & 2 & n^2-\beta \\ 3r-2 & 3 & \frac{n(3n-1)}{2} \end{vmatrix}$. Then $2A_{10}-A_8$ is :
questions.key_idea: $R_2-2R_1$ makes the second row $(0,0,\cdot)$, so $A_r$ does not depend on $r$ (or $n$).
solution: Apply $R_2\to R_2-2R_1$: the second row becomes $\left(0,\ 0,\ n^2-\beta-n^2-2\alpha\right)=(0,0,-\beta-2\alpha)$.
Expand along the second row (only the $(2,3)$ entry is non-zero, cofactor sign $-$): $A_r=(\beta+2\alpha)\left(3r-(3r-2)\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line reads '$=A_{10}=4\alpha+2\alpha$'; it should be $4\alpha+2\beta$ (as in its previous line $A_r=4\alpha+2\beta$). Answer (A) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Column operation instead: $C_1\to C_1-rC_2$ makes the first column $(0,0,-2)^{T}$, so the determinant no longer contains $r$ and a single cofactor remains.
solution: The first two columns are $(r,2r,3r-2)^{T}$ and $(1,2,3)^{T}$: note $(r,2r,3r)^{T}=r(1,2,3)^{T}$.
Apply $C_1\to C_1-rC_2$: the first column becomes $(0,\,0,\,-2)^{T}$.
Expand along the first column: $A_r=-2\cdot\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \frac{n^2}{2}+\alpha \\ 2 & n^2-\beta \end{vmatrix}=-2\left(n^2-\beta-n^2-2\alpha\right)=2\beta+4\alpha$.
The result is free of $r$ and $n$, so $2A_{10}-A_8=A_{10}=4\alpha+2\beta$. Same answer.

useful_results: If a determinant depends on a parameter $r$ only through one row/column and that row/column can be reduced by an operation involving another row/column, $r$ drops out - look for $r\cdot(\text{column})$ patterns.
Entries $(r,2r,3r-2)$ and $(1,2,3)$: $C_1-rC_2$ leaves the constants $(0,0,-2)$.
Whenever a question asks for $2A_{10}-A_8$ (or similar) with the same determinant for different $r$, suspect $A_r$ is constant.

$7x+11y-9z=2$
$97x+155y-189z=\mu$

questions.question: Let $\alpha\beta\gamma=45$; $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x(\alpha,1,2)+y(1,\beta,2)+z(2,3,\gamma)=(0,0,0)$ for some $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}$, $xyz\neq0$, then $6\alpha+4\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $xyz\neq0$ gives a non-trivial solution of a homogeneous system, so its determinant is $0$ and contains $\alpha\beta\gamma$.
solution: The vector equation gives the homogeneous system $\alpha x+y+2z=0$, $x+\beta y+3z=0$, $2x+2y+\gamma z=0$.
Since $xyz\neq0$, the solution is non-trivial, so $\begin{vmatrix} \alpha & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & \beta & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & \gamma \end{vmatrix}=0$.
useful_results: $xyz\neq0$ (or just $(x,y,z)\neq(0,0,0)$) in a homogeneous system means a non-trivial solution, i.e. $\det=0$.

The determinant of $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & \beta & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & \gamma \end{pmatrix}$ is $\alpha\beta\gamma-6\alpha-4\beta-\gamma+10$: the given product $\alpha\beta\gamma=45$ is meant to be substituted.
Equivalent statement: the three vectors $(\alpha,1,2),(1,\beta,2),(2,3,\gamma)$ are linearly dependent (coplanar), i.e. their scalar triple product is $0$.
Check with a valid triple: $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(1,1,45)$ has $\alpha\beta\gamma=45$ and $\det=45-6-4-45+10=0$; then $6\alpha+4\beta+\gamma=6+4+45=55$ ✓.
